1:
The date is fixed by another man's ministry. Gill names the month and observes that this was two months from Haggai's first prophecy and a few days after his second; Wesley says the same. Clarke adds that the two with united zeal encouraged the people to go on with the work of the temple, discontinued for some years. Calvin makes the pairing deliberate: the two were joined by God to confirm each other's doctrine, since they had to do with a refractory people enduring hard trials, who needed more than a common testimony. Henry draws encouragement from the sequence, that the people having been readily obedient to the word in the first prophet's mouth, God blessed them with another, for to him that has and uses well what he has, more shall be given. He also notices what the dating confesses. Before the captivity the prophets dated by the reigns of their own kings, and now by the kings to whom they were subjects, so melancholy a change had sin made in their circumstances.

Whose son the prophet was is asked next. Keil and Delitzsch takes him for son of Berechiah and grandson of Iddo, and explains why he is elsewhere called son of Iddo: he followed his grandfather in the priestly office, from which it is justly concluded that he returned from exile while still a youth and his father died young. Clarke reports that some maintain he was a priest and others deny it, and that many make him the immediate son of Iddo while others, with much more reason, his grandson. Ellicott holds that the title of prophet in the heading belongs, in spite of the accents, to Zechariah himself. He settles the name too: not remembrance of God, as Jerome took it, nor God's renown, but he whom God remembers.

The identification with a murdered namesake is sharper. Wesley says probably this is the Zechariah slain between the temple and the altar. Clarke will have none of it: the prophet has been confounded with a man of similar name in an earlier reign, and with the father of the forerunner, which is plainly incongruous, and thought to be the man our Saviour mentions as killed between temple and altar, though no such thing is anywhere said of him. Calvin agrees that those identifying him with the man of that name in the older history are mistaken.

On the message Calvin distinguishes two ways the word of God comes to men. God addresses all from the least to the greatest, but first sends his word to his prophets, to whom he commits the office of teaching; so it came to Zechariah not that he might keep it to himself but that he might dispense it faithfully. Ellicott notes that the ground of the exhortation lies in what is said of the fathers, the prophet himself included in that pronoun. Keil and Delitzsch marks the same structure, the warning being supported by an allusion to the fate the fathers brought on themselves. Gill says the displeasure was made manifest by the captivity and is a caution to the children not to follow the example. Clarke reads the summons as a proof of ability: it shews they had power to return if they would use it, and men are lost because they turn not to God, none for want of power, since God gives it and will require it. Ellicott is more careful: the words need not imply any special backsliding since the rebuilding began, when the Lord had declared he was with them, but rather that the more sincerely they turned the more gloriously his merciful intentions would be revealed; still, it may be seen how great need they had of repentance, and he quotes a writer comparing the prophet to the forerunner, warning from the history of the fathers that no spiritual privileges profit without holiness.
4:
The warning is drawn from an example rather than a rule. Gill says the fathers meant are those who lived before the captivity, who misused the prophets, despised his word and fell into gross idolatry, and takes the lesson to be that the evil examples of ancestors are not to be followed. Ellicott fixes who the former prophets were, those who prophesied while the city was still inhabited and prosperous, and notes that the old Greek here misplaces the qualifying word so that it attaches to the fathers rather than the prophets.

The two questions that follow are the crux, and how they are distributed changes everything. Clarke takes both as the prophet's own and answers both: the northern kingdom was ruined in the wars with one empire and the southern in those with another, so the fathers are gone; and the prophets too are dead, but their predictions remain, and the events which came about according to them prove that God sent them. Wesley reads them the same way, that the disobedient fathers were consumed with famine and sword as threatened, and that the prophets died as other men and must not live always to warn the living. Gill answers only the first, that the fathers are not in the land of the living, having perished by the sword or died in captivity. Ellicott divides the verse between two speakers. The prophet asks where the fathers are, meaning they perished through their iniquity; the people answer with the second question, that the prophets, who did not sin, are dead too, so what is the argument worth? On this reading the verse is an objection raised against the preacher rather than a second illustration offered by him.

What follows is then the reply to that objection. Ellicott states it directly: it is true that both the fathers and the former prophets are dead, but for all that the words of the prophets were actually fulfilled in the fathers, as the fathers themselves confessed. He reports this as the interpretation of an early rabbinic authority, and sets against it another view, that the sense is rather that the light of prophecy is dying out, so that while they have the light they should walk as children of the light; that interpretation, he says, destroys the prophet's argument. Gill takes the words and statutes for the predictions God ordered his prophets to declare in his name, that the fathers should die by sword or famine or pestilence or be carried captive. Wesley distinguishes the two terms, the first being the dreadful menaces spoken and the second the decreed judgments God resolved to execute and proclaimed by his prophets.

The verbs are weighed one by one. Ellicott prefers decrees to statutes, and notes that the old Greek inserts a word of command after it and adds a phrase probably carried in from a later chapter. On the next verb he prefers the marginal overtake, and observes that the Greek may here be a corruption of a negative. Wesley gives the same sense in a picture, that the words overtook them as a pursuing enemy overtakes and seizes the man he chases. Clarke reads the clause as an admission wrung from them, that everything happened according to the predictions and they were obliged to acknowledge it, and yet would not turn from their evil way. Ellicott prefers turned to returned in the following clause, taking it of repentance, and Wesley draws an inference from the narrative pause there, that it should seem the prophet gave them time to consider what answer they would make; the answer, when it came, was that as the Lord said he would do, so he had done.
7:
The new date is measured from the last. Clarke says the revelation came three months after the former and two months after the people recommenced building the temple, and places the month in the early part of the year. Ellicott adds that the month names in this book are of Assyrio-Babylonian origin and in use among the Jews to this day, and explains why the formula about the word of the Lord coming suits nocturnal visions: their substance was a divine revelation, and their meaning reached the prophet by the angel speaking to him. Henry gives the reason for the change of method, that God chose to speak by visions to awaken attention, engage reverence and enquiry, and fix the word in their memories; the visions seem designed for the comfort of a people newly returned from captivity and their encouragement to go on with the temple, and the scope of this first is to assure them of God's care when they seemed deserted. He also links it to the earlier sermon: the call to repentance having had good effect, God confirmed the assurances by returning to them in a way of mercy.

Whether the night is a symbol is disputed. Gill takes it as significant, a proper time for visions which may also denote their obscurity and the state of the church. Clarke agrees, that the time was emblematical of the affliction under which the people groaned. Ellicott denies it: the phrase means on this night, and it was during that night that the prophet saw the whole series; it does not mean that in his vision it appeared to be night. He adds that the seeing was not in a dream but, as a later chapter shews, in an ecstatic vision while awake.

Who the rider is receives two answers. Clarke takes him for an angel in the form of a man, supposed to have been the Lord Jesus, who seems often to have appeared so as a prelude to his incarnation, probably the same who appeared with a drawn sword as captain of the Lord's host. Wesley says simply Christ in the shape of a man, riding in readiness, posted like a captain at the head of his soldiers. Ellicott declines that identification: the construction of the Hebrew shews beyond controversy that the man standing among the myrtles and the angel of the Lord named a few verses later are the same, and angels assuming human form are often called men. He prefers bay to red for the horse, and renders the place a certain hollow, as Keil and Delitzsch renders the same word.

What the details mean divides confident from cautious. Clarke reads the red as an emblem of war and the myrtle as an emblem of peace, intimating that all war was shortly to end, though some take the trees for the true followers of Christ; the horses behind point out the orders of angels employed in the church's defence, their colours marking gradations in power. Wesley reads the colour as a symbol of coming vengeance, the trees as fragrant emblems of the saints, the low ground as the church in affliction, the red of the following horses as the bloody condition of kingdoms at war, and the speckled as a mixed colour, an emblem perhaps of affairs neither all dark nor all light. Ellicott sets out the same field from the outside, observing that commentators attach special significance to the myrtles in the hollow, some seeing in the trees the pious and others the land, and taking the hollow for the place of exile or the degradation into which the people had fallen; the colours are treated the same way, some making them the lands the riders were sent to, others three successive empires, others the various missions. He offers these as specimens, and is clear only that the horses mean horses with riders.
9:
Who is addressed in the question is the first thing to settle, and the answers diverge. Clarke says the angel here mentioned was distinct from those named in the verse before, being the one who talked with the prophet. Ellicott identifies him as the angel-interpreter, whose office it was to interpret the visions and who is often referred to afterwards simply as he; he notes that the phrase may be rendered the angel that talked in me rather than with me, and that the old Greek reads it so. Wesley takes the address quite differently, as made to Christ, the Lord of hosts, and identifies the angel with Christ, the angel of the covenant. Gill says only that the words are the prophet's to the angel who shewed him the vision.

The answer comes from an unexpected quarter, and Gill makes something of that. The man standing among the myrtle trees answers, and so prevents the angel from giving the account he was about to give; he was more capable of giving it, and to do so was great condescension in him and a singular honour done to the prophet. Ellicott adds a caution about the verb: the word rendered answered need not imply that any question had been asked at all, since like the corresponding Greek word it often means merely that a speaker began to speak. He also settles which angel is meant in the following verse, that it is the man riding on the bay horse, and fixes the scope of the word rendered earth: it means the world, the whole earth, and not merely the land, which is often the sense of the same word elsewhere.

Who the riders are is agreed with small differences of emphasis. Wesley calls them angels, ministers of divine providence in the government of the world. Clarke calls them guardians constituted over the land. Gill takes them for the ministering angels signified by the horses of the several colours, replying to what had been said of them, or rather confirming that account, or else rendering up the account of their tour through the earth with their observations on the state of it. Ellicott gives them a sharper function: they had been sent forth to act, as it were, as scouts, and to bring back an account of the state of the world, so that at the intercession of the angel of the Lord comforting words might be announced to the prophet and by him to the people.

What they report is the same in words and not in sense. Clarke reads it as a plain political fact: there was general peace through the empire and the states connected with the province, but the people themselves were still in affliction, their city not yet restored nor their temple built. Wesley reads it as ease, that all men sit still to take their rest and all is peaceable, this being the state of the empire which at that time ruled all. Ellicott will not let the rest pass as neutral. The world is reported still and at rest, that is, dwelling in self-confident security; and he sets that against a prophecy delivered only two months before, that God would shake the heavens and the earth and overthrow the throne of kingdoms. The overthrow so foretold had not yet begun, and it is that gap between the promise and the quiet which the vision is answering. On this reading the calm of the nations is not the good news it sounds but the very thing that makes the question of the next verse urgent.
12:
The intercession is the turn of the vision. Gill identifies the speaker as the angel who stood among the myrtle trees; Clarke identifies him with the Lord Jesus and makes it an instance of a standing office, Christ being always the sole Mediator between God and man. Ellicott says the angel of the Lord intercedes for the city and the cities of the province.

The seventy years named in that plea are the difficulty, and two reckonings are offered, both rejecting the obvious one. Clarke says the number cannot mean the duration of the captivity, that being nearly twenty years past; it must mean the time from the destruction of the temple to the moment the angel spoke, and since the temple fell in the nineteenth year of one king and this vision came in the second year of another, the term was then complete. Ellicott works from the other end. The English phrase renders one Hebrew word often used as a round number; from the first taking of the city to the decree that sent the people home is sixty-eight years, and those are the seventy years foretold by the earlier prophet. But eighteen years had passed since that decree, so the actual figure was eighty-eight, and the intercessor can hardly have meant that period; most probably, he concludes, the reference is to a span running from a later taking of the city.

Who receives the answer is noticed by all three. Ellicott observes that the Lord does not reply to the intercessor but addresses the interpreting angel, who at once delivers the message of comfort; Clarke says the angel told the prophet the answer was gracious; Gill that its effect was communicated to a ministering angel and by him to the prophet. On the jealousy Clarke glosses it as strong affection for the people and indignation against their enemies. Ellicott presses the tense: the verb is perfect, like the one rendered I am returned, denoting that the Lord had already shewn his jealous love in bringing them out of captivity and would shew it still in completing the restoration.

The clause about being a little displeased reads two ways. Wesley takes it of degree, that God was but little displeased with his own people compared with the anger he bears the nations, and reads the next clause as saying they attempted to destroy those he meant only to correct. Clarke says the same, that he gave their enemies a commission against them, but they carried it far beyond his design, and shall now suffer in their turn. Ellicott allows degree but offers duration as an alternative, for a little while, and prefers helped for evil to helped forward the affliction, meaning they not only chastised as God's instruments but wished to annihilate; the old Greek, he notes, reads of nations that combine to set upon the people where the English has nations at ease. Gill names the nations concerned, then free from war and prosperous while the people were low.

The promises are read literally. Clarke says the principal mercy is that the house of the Lord shall be rebuilt and its ordinances re-established, the circuit determined and the city built to the line marked out; Ellicott says the line is to measure the confines, Wesley that it marks out walls, gates, streets and houses. On the last promise Ellicott prefers filled to overflowing, and observes that the same verb in the same conjugation is used elsewhere of being scattered in a bad sense, its ordinary use, though another conjugation means spreading without that colour. Clarke reads it of the whole land inhabited and the ruined cities restored, and Wesley of increase, families multiplying until they send out colonies and plant new cities. Gill notes that the command to cry again means, as one old paraphrase gives it, to prophesy again and publish openly.
18:
The horns are read as powers. Ellicott says the horn is a symbol of power and hostility and the four denote the nations which had oppressed the people; Wesley calls them powers and kingdoms which had from all sides pushed at and tossed them. Henry works the figure hard: they tossed the people as furious bulls toss what they are enraged at, and scattered them so that no man lifted up his head, none daring to shew his face, much less to make head against them; the horn denotes dignity and dominion, the horn exalted strength and violence; and they are four because the people were surrounded, so that avoiding one horn they ran upon another. Clarke names four oppressing powers, and offers as an alternative that the number is owing to the four cardinal points they came from, assigning peoples to each.

Ellicott opposes the commonest identification, and argues from grammar. Many commentators, he says, suppose the vision to look forward as well as back, combining its objects into one picture without regard to the time of their appearing, and so take the horns for the four great empires. That cannot be, and this verse shews it. The word rendered scattered, standing alone, might serve at once as historic and prophetic perfect; but the dependent clause about no man lifting up his head is also perfect, so the scattering can refer only to the past. Every reference to the usual four monarchies must therefore be rejected, since the last had not yet come into existence; if the horns symbolise monarchies at all they can only be the four already in the field. He extends the caution to the workmen, saying some identify them with four named rulers, whereas it seems more probable that here, as in the earlier vision, symbol and thing symbolised must not be too closely compared. He also loosens the verb, observing that scattered need not mean dispersal into captivity but may mean the national unity was broken up, and notes that the two names joined to Judah define it rather than add to it.

What the workmen are called turns on a Hebrew word. Ellicott says workmen is better than carpenters, since the word does not mean carpenters unless followed by the word for wood. Gill prefers blacksmiths, since the horns were iron and the same word is rendered smith elsewhere, signifying a worker in wood or iron indifferently. Clarke reports a correspondent who takes the root back further, to silent thought or attention, and so to contriving in silence, whence it is applied to an artificer of any kind and to work requiring close attention, such as the ploughman's, who must give heed to keep a straight furrow; on that ground he would render it watchers. Gill notes that the prophet, seeing artificers, concluded there was work for them.

Who they are is answered three ways. Clarke makes them four powers who should defeat those meant by the horns, identifies them with the four chariots of a later vision, and names a ruler for each, some already cast down and the rest to come. Gill reports two Jewish lists making them expected deliverers, and prefers an expositor who takes them for the princes above who preside over kingdoms, that is the angels, noting that two early writers took the same view. Wesley keeps it general: they are emblems of the instruments God will employ to break those destroyers. Henry sets the vision under a text he takes as its key, that when the enemy comes in like a flood the Spirit of the Lord lifts a standard against him, and reads it as the Spirit making a stand against the power of the church's adversaries. On the verb describing what they do, Clarke says it means to break, pound and reduce to powder, and derives the English word from a French verb meaning rub.
